title: Cap. 1 subject: sin-infection debated — Scotus / Suarez before foresight
pass_a_gloss: There is another quality or condition which most judge to be necessarily prerequisite and presupposed in the act of Predestinating and Reprobating, but it is not so much in confession among all: But this is the infection of Sin, which they think foreseen by God in the subject, before it can either be predestined or reprobated. From the opinion of these therefore, in order that these acts be terminated unto a creature, it does not suffice that it be rational, but it is also presupposed that it be a sinner, or stained with sin. Not gladly would I make this controversy mine; yet in a few words I will open what is thought by others, and what I myself think. It must therefore necessarily be confessed by us that that opinion is not recently born, or of ignoble Theologians, which places predestination prior to the foresight of sin. Indeed nearly all who through predestination understood not so much the preparation of means, as a mere designation unto the end itself, have philosophized in this mode. Scotus, where he assigns the order of instants in the Divine mind and will, always established the will of giving beatitude to be prior to the foresight of the fall, Book 1 distinction 41 unique question; and book 3 distinction 19 question 1 he places that God in the first instant willed glory for a determined number of the elect, in the second ordered grace for them, in the third foresaw them about to fall in Adam. Now when I say Scotus was in this opinion, you understand also that others as many as you will, who wish to be held Scotists, sensed the same. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and innumerable others teach the decree of predestination to be prior not only to the decree of permitting the fall, but even to that of creating the human being. These therefore do not think foreseen sin to be a condition, or quality of the subject, into which the act of predestination ought to fall. Finally, from the recent Jesuits, Suarez himself follows this opinion, and testifies it to be common, in these words: I judge more probable the common opinion of Theologians asserting that the election of predestined human beings preceded the permission of original sin.
pass_b_english: Another quality most writers treat as necessarily presupposed in predestinating and reprobating — though not all agree: the infection of sin, which they think God foresaw in the subject before it could be predestined or reprobated. On their view rationality is not enough; the creature must also be presupposed a sinner, stained with sin. I do not gladly make this quarrel my own; still I will open briefly what others hold and what I hold. We must admit that the opinion which puts predestination before foresight of sin is neither new nor the property of obscure theologians. Nearly everyone who took predestination as bare designation to the end itself, rather than preparation of means, reasoned this way. Scotus, ordering instants in the Divine mind and will, always set the will to give beatitude before foresight of the fall (I dist. 41; III dist. 19 q.1): God first wills glory for a fixed number of elect, next orders grace for them, then foresees their fall in Adam. With Scotus stand many who claim the Scotist name. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and countless others teach the decree of predestination prior even to permitting the fall — and prior to creating man. So they do not treat foresight of sin as a condition of the subject on which predestination falls. Among recent Jesuits Suarez follows the same line and calls it the common opinion: I judge more probable the theologians' common view that the election of the predestined preceded permission of original sin.
source_text: Est altera qualitas sive conditio quam plerique arbitrantur necessario prerequiri & praesupponi in actu Praedestinandi & Reprobandi, sed non est tam in confesso apud omnes: Haec autem est Peccati infectio, quam a Deo praevisam putant in subjecto, priusquam vel praedestinari vel reprobari possit. Ex horum igitur sententia, ut actus hi terminentur ad creaturam, non sufficit quod rationalis sit, sed etiam praesupponitur quod peccatrix, sive peccato coinquinata sit. Haud lubens hanc litem meam fecerim; paucis tamen quid ab aliis sentiatur, & quid ipse sentiam, aperiam. Est itaque nobis necessario fatendum, non esse nuper natam, aut ignobilium Theologorum sententiam, quae ponit praedestinationem priorem praevisione peccati. Imo omnes fere qui per praedestinationem intellexerunt non tam mediorum praeparationem, quam meram designationem ad ipsum finem, hoc modo philosophati sunt. Scotus ubi assignat ordinem instantium in mente & voluntate Divina, semper statuit priorem esse voluntatem dandi beatitudinem praevisione lapsus, Lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. unica; & lib. 3. dist. 19. qu. 1. ponit Deum in primo instanti voluisse gloriam determinato numero electorum, in secundo ordinasse illis gratiam, in tertio praevidisse eos lapsuros in Adamo. Jam cum dico Scotum in hac sententia fuisse, intelligitis & alios quam plurimos, qui Scotistae haberi volunt, idem sensisse. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonfus Mendoza, aliique innumeri decretum praedestinationis, non solum decreto lapsus permittendi, sed etiam hominis creandi, prius esse docent. Hi ergo non putant peccatum praevisum esse conditionem, aut qualitatem subjecti, in quod cadere debet actus praedestinationis. Postremo, ex Jesuitis neotericis, ipse Suarez hanc sententiam sequitur, & communem esse testatur, hisce verbis: Probabiliorem existimo communem sententiam Theologorum asserentium, electionem hominum praedestinatorum antecessisse permissionem originalis peccati.
